idiom_name: module of async functions over global fetch with an injected connection function
implementation_notes: In JavaScript the gateway is usually not a class at all: a module exports a small set of async functions named in the application's language, calls the global fetch API, and returns objects already in domestic shape - which is exactly Fowler's JavaScript example, where the gateway is a function and the connection is a function passed in. Translating the awkward parts (equipment codes, millisecond versus minute parameters, string dates, nested response objects) happens in those few lines, so call sites read like business code. Reach for a class only when several methods share mutable state such as an auth token or a cursor, and in that case keep injection: take the fetch implementation (or a connection function) as a constructor/default parameter so tests can pass a stub.
pitfalls: fetch resolves for HTTP error statuses: a gateway that skips res.ok turns a 500 into a confusing parse failure deep inside business code.
A response body is a stream and can be consumed once; a logging or telemetry layer that also wants the body must clone it (res.clone()).
Never hide an unbounded loop of fetches behind one method, and keep the connection injectable - mocking the global fetch or the module is fragile and usually hides missing translation.
Timers and AbortSignal: without an explicit signal and timeout a slow foreign service keeps the request (and its promise chain) alive indefinitely.
